h1: Palate cleansers for beer tastings: water, crackers or bread
title: Palate Cleansers for Beer Tastings | Craft Beer School
desc: Which palate cleansers work for beer tastings: water, unsalted crackers, plain bread and what to avoid, with tips for home tastings and formal panels.
teaser: Water, crackers or bread? The right palate cleanser keeps every beer tasting like itself. The wrong one makes them all taste like peanuts.
standfirst: A palate cleanser resets your mouth between beers so each sample gets a fair hearing. The best ones are boring on purpose. Here is what works, what does not and how to set up a tasting table.
sections: What a palate cleanser should do

Between beers, your mouth holds on to the last one: bitterness on the tongue, acidity, sweetness, fat and aroma at the back of the throat. A good cleanser removes these traces without adding any of its own.

The ideal cleanser is neutral in taste, neutral in smell, low in salt and low in fat. It should be easy to eat quickly and should not fill you up. Anything with strong flavour of its own leaves another trace behind.
Water: the first and best choice

Plain water at room temperature is the standard on every judging table. Cold water numbs the tongue briefly, which can make the next beer seem flatter. Very hot water is unpleasant and shocks the palate.

Still water is better than sparkling, since carbonation adds its own sharp feel. Use filtered or bottled water with a neutral taste. Some municipal and borewell water in India carries a chlorine or mineral note that you will notice next to delicate beer, so taste the water first. If it smells of chlorine, use filtered water instead.

Rinse, swish and either swallow or spit. A sip of water between each beer is enough for most tastings.

Plain, unsalted water crackers are the other classic. Their dry, starchy texture absorbs bitterness and oils from the tongue and gently scrubs the palate. Professional panels commonly use them alongside water.

Choose the plainest crackers you can find, ideally with no salt on the surface, no butter and no seasoning. Many cream crackers and salted crackers are too salty. Salt changes how bitterness and sweetness are perceived, which defeats the point.

Plain white bread, with or without crust, works almost as well as crackers. Its soft texture is good for absorbing acidity and bitterness. Many home tasters find it easier to source than unsalted crackers.

Avoid flavoured breads, seeded loaves, sourdough with strong tang or anything buttered. A slice of plain pav or a simple sandwich loaf is ideal. Plain idli or plain rice cakes can also work. They are neutral, low in fat and easy to find in Indian kitchens.

• Salted snacks. Peanuts, chips and namkeen make beer taste sweeter and rounder and leave salt on the palate.
  • Fried food. Fat coats the tongue and kills beer foam if it reaches the glass.
  • Cheese. Delicious with beer, but not a cleanser. It coats the palate with fat and flavour.
  • Spicy food. Chilli heat stays for minutes and makes bitterness and alcohol feel stronger.
  • Strong flavours. Pickles, olives, citrus and mint all leave their own trace.
  • Coffee and tea. Bitter and aromatic, they confuse the palate.

Save these for after the tasting, or for a separate food pairing session where they are the point.
Matching the cleanser to the beer

Different beers leave different traces, so a little adjustment helps. After a hoppy IPA, bitterness clings to the tongue. A cracker does more than water alone. After a sour beer, acidity lingers, so plain bread helps absorb it. After a stout, roast and sweetness coat the mouth. A good rinse of water followed by a cracker clears it.

Alcohol needs time more than food. After a strong beer, wait a couple of minutes before the next sample, rinse with water and do not rush. Some tasters like a slice of plain cucumber after a run of strong beers. It is cool and watery with very little flavour, though it is not standard on judging tables.

Whatever you choose, use the same cleanser for every taster and every beer in the session. Changing it halfway through makes the later beers taste different for reasons that have nothing to do with the beer.

For each taster, put out a jug or bottle of room temperature water, a glass for water, a small plate of plain crackers or bread and a spit cup. Space beers so there is time between samples. A minute or two to rinse and reset is enough for most beers. Give a little longer after strong, bitter or sour samples.

In a home tasting, the cleanser also slows the pace, which keeps the evening responsible. Our guide to setting up a beer tasting covers the rest of the table. For formal panels, consistency matters most: use the same water, the same crackers and the same timing every session. Our guide to running a sensory panel covers that discipline. A cleanser does its job only if everyone uses it the same way. That kind of method is part of what a sensory course drills.
faqs: What is the best palate cleanser for beer?
Room temperature still water, with plain unsalted crackers or plain white bread. They reset the palate without adding flavours of their own.
Can I use salted snacks between beers?
It is best not to. Salt changes how sweet and bitter a beer seems and leaves its own trace, so save salted snacks for after the tasting.
No. Room temperature water is better. Cold water numbs the tongue briefly and can make the next beer taste flatter.
